items.target_specification: Full models support emphatic agreement; do not mistake self for an invariant pronoun.

items.prompt: Give the strong masculine accusative singular, feminine genitive singular, neuter nominative plural and dative plural of sum, ǣnig, gehwilc and swilc.
items.target_specification: Apply each complete indefinite paradigm across cases, genders and numbers.

items.prompt: Give the complete singular and plural declension of līf. Explain why the plural in “our lives” is an ordinary contextual plural in this unit.
items.target_specification: Complete noun paradigm with explicit plural-form promotion and actual plural sense.

items.prompt: Give the complete present and preterite indicative of ætēowian, then the singular and plural present and preterite subjunctive. State which persons each subjunctive entry covers.
items.target_specification: Complete new finite systems, not isolated recall of the Cook wish form.

items.prompt: Give the singular and plural present and preterite subjunctive of scīnan, stating which persons each entry covers. Then give both second-person commands of geblētsian and identify the number of people addressed.
items.target_specification: Complete newly assigned systems required by Cook I.8.15–17; a familiar indicative or a supplied source cell does not establish the remaining forms.

items.prompt: Turn each statement into a yes/no question: Hē hæfð scip. Ðā męnn sindon gōde. Ðū gesāwe ðæt scip. Preserve person, number and tense.
items.target_specification: Direct question formation with finite verb and subject; no English do-support.

items.prompt: Translate into Old English: Who has that ship? Whom does the man see? What does the man have? State the case of each interrogative.
items.target_specification: Subject, personal object and neuter object case in meaningful questions.

items.prompt: Translate into Old English: To whom do you (sing.) give that fish? Whose ship do you (sing.) see? Explain what governs each interrogative case.
items.target_specification: Dative recipient and genitive possessor; familiar noun forms retain external case.

items.prompt: Two men are being compared. Ask “Which of the two men has that ship?” using attributive hwæðer with singular mann. Then ask “What sort of ship is that?” using hūlic.
items.target_specification: Bounded attributive which-of-two and quality question; no unintroduced partitive phrase.

items.prompt: Translate Hū swimð se mann? and Hwȳ swimð se mann? Explain the difference in the information requested.
items.target_specification: Lexical how/why, without general instrumental production.

items.prompt: Ask “Do you (sing.) have any fish?” using ǣnig and singular fisc. A learner adds dōn because English uses do; explain why that addition is unnecessary.
items.target_specification: Direct question with an indefinite and no mechanical English auxiliary transfer.

items.prompt: Translate Sum mann hæfð scip and Sume męnn habbað scipu. Identify the subject and object forms and explain the change in number.
items.target_specification: Attributive sum in singular/plural; ordinary possession and full agreement.

items.prompt: Translate: Each man sees a ship. Use gehwilc and singular mann. Then replace “each man” with “each companion” without changing the meaning of the verb.
items.target_specification: Ordinary singular distributive use; noun gender/case and verbal agreement.

items.prompt: Translate: The other man has another ship. Use ōðer twice. Explain why “other/another” is not automatically “second” here.
items.target_specification: New other sense with the already taught strong morphology.

items.prompt: Translate: I saw the same man. I give the fish to the same man. Use ilca and give the case of each complete noun phrase.
items.target_specification: Weak-only same under article in accusative and dative.

items.prompt: Translate Hē self geseah ðæt scip. Then translate “I save myself,” spoken by a man, using mē selfne. Distinguish emphasis on the subject from a reflexive object.
items.target_specification: Strong self agreement with nominative subject versus accusative object; existing nęrian frame.

items.prompt: Translate Swilce męnn sindon gōde. Explain how the inflected word swilce differs from the invariant adverb swilce “likewise.”
items.target_specification: Indefinite such versus prior adverb; no automatic word-class inference from spelling.

items.prompt: Give a full Old English noun phrase for each: of some men (genitive); to any companion (dative); that same ship (accusative); such little birds (accusative). Label the case and relevant agreement.
items.target_specification: Genitive/dative/accusative application with indefinites, same and ordinary strong adjective agreement.

items.prompt: Join Se mann is gōd and Se mann hæfð ðæt scip into one sentence with ðe meaning “The man who has that ship is good.” Identify the relative subject.
items.target_specification: Invariant subject relative; noun predicate remains in main clause.

items.prompt: Join Ic geseah ðæt scip and Se mann hæfð ðæt scip into one sentence with ðe. Retain “I saw” as the main clause.
items.target_specification: Invariant object relative with its own nominative subject.

items.prompt: Combine Ic sęlle ðone fisc ðǣm męnn and Se mann mē healp. Use an inflected demonstrative followed by ðe for the relative. Label the antecedent case and relative case separately.
items.target_specification: Dative antecedent, nominative relative and dative object of helpan.

items.prompt: Combine Ic geseah ðone mann and Ic healp ðǣm męnn. Use an inflected demonstrative followed by ðe. Explain why the two references to the man have different cases.
items.target_specification: Accusative antecedent, dative relative governed by helpan.

items.prompt: Translate: You (sing.), who helped me, give me that fish. Use ðe and the preterite of helpan; identify the relative verb’s person and the command’s person.
items.target_specification: Second-person relative agreement and second-singular imperative.

items.prompt: Change the addressee of your L5 sentence to two or more people. Change every affected pronoun and finite verb, keeping the fish singular.
items.target_specification: Plural personal antecedent controls relative and command agreement.

items.prompt: In Se mann, ðe ðæt scip hæfð, is mīn gefēra and Ic geseah ðæt scip, ðe se mann hæfð, identify each antecedent and each relative role. Does ðe itself change its spelling to show those roles? Then translate Se mann, ðæs scip ic geseah, is gōd and explain the case and function of ðæs and scip.
items.target_specification: Invariant subject/object relatives, followed by a concrete possessive relative with separately governed antecedent, relative and possessed-noun cases.

items.prompt: A learner says that an inflected relative must always have the same case as its antecedent. Correct that rule using L3 or L4. State the ordinary production target and the limited exception noted in the lesson.
items.target_specification: Internal-clause case is the selected target; source-attested case attraction is not denied.

items.prompt: Translate: They finish the work. They fill the waters. Use gefyllan in both sentences and explain the difference of sense.
items.target_specification: Prior finish sense versus newly promoted fill sense, same known morphology.

items.prompt: Translate: The man has all the animals in his control. Use on with the appropriate form of geweald and an invariant possessor. Then make it a command to one person, “Have all the animals in your control.”
items.target_specification: Habban ... on one’s geweald idiom and singular command; distinguish from spatial under.

items.prompt: Translate: I live my life. We live our lives. State the case and number of each object and explain why libban can have that object here.
items.target_specification: Bounded cognate accusative and deliberate ordinary plural life sense.

items.prompt: Translate: Dry land appears. Let dry land appear. Use ætēowian and identify the mood of each verb.
items.target_specification: New complete finite system applied to assertion and wish.

items.prompt: Translate the complete account “The ship and the fish.” Keep the speakers and the three men’s relationships clear.
items.target_specification: Independent connected reading using taught material.

items.prompt: In the account, list the direct questions. For each interrogative, give its role and the information requested.
items.target_specification: Question form, case and meaning in connected context.

items.prompt: In the answer beginning Ic sęlle, explain the roles and cases of hine, ðǣm męnn, se and mē. What identifies the man receiving the fish?
items.target_specification: Distinct object, recipient, relative subject and helped person; contextual identification without invented names.

items.prompt: Rewrite the final answer so that the man has two little ships which you (sing.) saw. Preserve its relative construction and change all necessary forms.
items.target_specification: Plural antecedent/demonstrative agreement and unchanged second-singular relative verb.

items.prompt: Translate the complete Merchant and Teacher excerpt using the local helps. Preserve who speaks each question and answer.
items.target_specification: Connected exact-source translation; supplied material does not become unaided recall.

items.prompt: Identify the direct questions in the excerpt and explain what each asks. Use the local help for the merchant’s form of address.
items.target_specification: Direct-question analysis within exact supported source.

items.prompt: In ðā on ðissum lande ne bēoð ācęnnede, identify the antecedent, the role of ðā and the number of the passive auxiliary. Use the supplied participle meaning.
items.target_specification: Demonstrative relative and known passive agreement with explicit new lexical support.

items.prompt: Using the local helps, explain how the merchant obtains his goods and where he takes them. Distinguish these statements from the dangers he encounters.
items.target_specification: Essential connected meaning and sequence of supported maritime clauses.

items.prompt: Identify two expressions for dangers in the final answer, and explain the contribution of the closing words unēaðe cwic ætberstende. Use the supplied meanings and construction notes.
items.target_specification: Source detail and explicitly supported accompanying-participle meaning.

items.prompt: Translate: Which men have the ships that you (sing.) saw? Use hwilc and ðe. Label the interrogative, antecedent and relative roles.
items.target_specification: Plural attributive interrogative with object relative and retained second-singular past.

items.prompt: Translate: I give another fish to the same man who helped me. Use ōðer, ilca and an inflected demonstrative followed by ðe.
items.target_specification: Other/same, giving dative and internally nominative relative.

items.prompt: Translate: Do you (sing.) see any little birds? Use ǣnig with plural fugol and the appropriate form of lȳtel.
items.target_specification: Direct question plus indefinite and strong adjective agreement.

items.prompt: Translate: Each companion himself saw that ship. Use gehwilc and strong self. Then make the whole statement a direct yes/no question.
items.target_specification: Distributive singular, emphatic agreement and question formation.

items.prompt: Translate: The man who has the ship says, “Let dry land appear.” Use ðe and retain a direct quotation.
items.target_specification: Relative subject, cweðan direct quotation and newly taught appearance wish.

items.prompt: Explain the different functions of ðæt in ðæt scip and ðæt ðe ðū gesāwe in the account. Does their identical spelling make both conjunctions meaning “that”?
items.target_specification: Demonstrative determiner versus relative pronoun; no accidental promotion of content conjunction.

items.prompt: Give the nominative, genitive, dative and accusative singular and plural of sunu. Distinguish the dative singular from the nominative and accusative singular.
items.target_specification: Complete newly assigned u-stem noun system, with every NGDA cell.

items.prompt: Give the complete present and preterite indicative of bycgan. Name all three persons in each number, including cells with identical spellings.
items.target_specification: Complete new indicative system and lexical dental-stem exception.

items.prompt: Give the singular and plural commands of rōwan and bycgan. State which forms address one person and which address more than one.
items.target_specification: Complete two-person command systems; stem alternations are lexical.

items.prompt: Give the nominative, genitive, dative and accusative singular and plural of rīce and geðeahtend. Identify the characteristic plural endings of each pattern.
items.target_specification: Complete new neuter -e and masculine -end noun patterns; lexical variants remain separate.

items.prompt: Translate the nominative noun phrase ‘the kingdoms of the counsellors’, placing the genitive dependent first and omitting a separate article for the head noun. Then translate ‘I give the fish (sing.) to the counsellors.’ Explain the different cases of ‘counsellors’.
items.target_specification: Meaningful use of the new nominal systems with earlier genitive and recipient government.

items.prompt: Classify every ðæt in these sentences as demonstrative/article, relative, or content conjunction. For each inflected occurrence, give its case and explain whether it agrees with a noun or functions within the relative clause. (a) Ðæt scip is gōd. (b) Ic wāt, ðæt ðæt scip gōd is. (c) Ðæt scip, ðæt ðū hæfst, is gōd.
items.target_specification: Separate homographic demonstrative, relative and content-conjunction functions.

items.prompt: Translate: I know that the ships are empty. Present their emptiness as an asserted fact and use the indicative in the content clause.
items.target_specification: Known factual finite content after witan, with plural agreement.

items.prompt: Se fiscere cwið: “Ic hæbbe twēgen fiscas.” Report his words beginning Se fiscere sægð and using ðæt with the present subjunctive. The fisherman is the possessor in both versions.
items.target_specification: Present reported content and reference change from quoted first person to reported third person.

items.prompt: Se mann cwæð: “Ic hæbbe twēgen fiscas.” Report the same state at the time of his past speech, beginning Se mann sægde. Use ðæt and the preterite subjunctive; the same man possessed the fish.
items.target_specification: Bounded simultaneous past report; reference changes do not alter the referent.

items.prompt: A task requests a subjunctive report, but a learner writes Hē sægð, ðæt hē gōd is. Is the sentence necessarily ungrammatical? Give the requested form and explain the distinction.
items.target_specification: Distinguish valid indicative reporting from compliance with an explicit subjunctive target.

items.prompt: Translate both clauses and explain the case of the question word. (a) Ic wāt, hwā ðone fisc hæbbe. (b) Ic wāt, hwǣm ðū ðone fisc sęlle.
items.target_specification: The question word's internal subject or recipient role determines its case.

items.prompt: Turn Hwæt hæfst ðū? into a dependent question after Saga mē. Keep the same addressee and use the present subjunctive.
items.target_specification: Dependent object question after tell, with dative recipient and internal accusative hwæt.

items.prompt: Turn Hæfð se mann twēgen fiscas? into a dependent yes/no question after Saga mē. Use hwæðer and the present subjunctive.
items.target_specification: Invariant whether introduces a dependent yes/no question.

items.prompt: Translate and distinguish the two uses of hwæðer. In (a), two men are under discussion. (a) Hwæðer mann is ðīn gefēra? (b) Saga mē, hwæðer se mann ðīn gefēra sīe.
items.target_specification: Earlier agreeing which-of-two adjective versus new invariant whether conjunction.

items.prompt: Translate: I know whom you (sing.) help. Use a dependent question with hwǣm and the present subjunctive.
items.target_specification: Preserve helpan's dative government inside a dependent question.

items.prompt: Translate both sentences and identify who carries the fish. (a) Ic wille ðone fisc beran. (b) Ic hāte hine ðone fisc beran. Explain why beran has no person ending in either sentence.
items.target_specification: Same-subject volition versus an independently expressed commanded actor.

items.prompt: The fisherman told two companions, “Berað ðone fisc.” Report this as a past command using hātan, hīe for the companions, and a plain infinitive.
items.target_specification: Reported command with plural accusative actor and invariant infinitive.

items.prompt: Translate: I see the men carrying the fish (sing.). Use gesēon with an accusative actor and a plain infinitive; label both accusative noun phrases.
items.target_specification: Perception complement with an actor distinct from the infinitive's object.

items.prompt: Translate both sentences using gewyrcean followed by an object and an agreeing predicate adjective: God made the man good. God made the men good. Explain the adjective endings.
items.target_specification: Strong predicate adjective agrees with an accusative object, independently of the article inside the object noun phrase.

items.prompt: Translate and distinguish the two complements: Hē hēt ðone mann cyning. Hē hēt ðone mann gān. State the case/function of cyning and the form/function of gān.
items.target_specification: Prior naming predicate versus newly assigned command infinitive.

items.prompt: You have no ship. Express the present unreal wish “Would that I had one ship!” using the preterite subjunctive of habban.
items.target_specification: A bounded present unreal wish; inflectional preterite does not require past time.

items.prompt: Translate these in their stated settings: (a) a report about last year, Ic hæfde ān scip.; (b) a wish by someone who has no ship now, Hæfde ic ān scip! Explain what the shared spelling hæfde can and cannot show.
items.target_specification: Context distinguishes past assertion from present unreal wish despite syncretic morphology.

local_support.text: Witodlice is a connective here (Cook gives Latin autem). Mannes Bearn means the Son of Man: mannes is genitive singular and Bearn neuter nominative singular. The subsequent hē/him/his refer to this male person.
In his glory/majesty. Mægenðrymme is dative masculine singular. This abstract expression is supplied as a whole.

local_support.source_expression: and ealle ęnglas samod mid him …
local_support.text: And all the angels together with him. The source leaves the coming verb understood in this coordinated part; the angels are nominative plural, not objects of with. Mid him separately means with him. Tō ðǣm miclan dōme means to the great judgment.
Then. Both occurrences are independent sentence adverbs sequencing the scene; they are not the previously taught than or subordinate when.
Throne/seat of his majesty. Mægenðrymnesse is a feminine genitive singular characterizing the throne; Cook note7 refers to the genitive of quality (§153.f).

local_support.source_expression: bēoð gegaderode ætforan him ealle ðēoda
local_support.text: All nations will be gathered before him. Bēoð is third-person plural, and ðēoda is the following nominative feminine plural subject. Gegaderode is the exact supplied plural passive participle; ætforan him means before him. Ealle is the feminine plural -e variant here; the ordinary selected target ealla remains valid.

Separates them into two groups. Tōscǣt is third-person singular present; hīe is its accusative plural object. On twā is the locally supplied divided-in-two expression; twā is neuter accusative plural here.

local_support.source_expression: swā-swā scēaphierde tōscǣt scēap fram gātum
local_support.text: Just as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. The whole comparative connection is supplied. Scēaphierde is the nominative subject, scēap the accusative plural object, and gātum dative after fram. The noun scēap has identical singular/plural nominative/accusative shapes; the source explicitly identifies this occurrence as plural.

local_support.source_expression: gelōgað … on his swīðran hand … on his winstran
local_support.text: He places the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left. Gelōgað is an exact supplied third-singular present. The two animal phrases are accusative plural objects. The right/left expressions share a placement frame; on takes accusative hand in this bounded right/left-side expression (the final hand is understood). The following unassigned source line8 uses the same expression with static standað; this is not a universal motion-versus-rest rule. Swīðran/winstran are weak feminine singular forms. Their -an alone does not distinguish accusative from dative; judge the complete clause and the bare hand form.

items.target_specification: Negative purpose, not negation of the main action or assertion of the feared outcome.

items.prompt: Translate and parse sīe. The speaker accepts that the man is sick: can the selected subjunctive still be used, and what relation does the clause express?
items.target_specification: Concession can concede a fact; subjunctive is not a synonym for false.

items.prompt: In (a), his presence is an open question. In (b), he is absent now. Translate both, identify their finite moods, and state the time referred to by wǣre and hulpe.
items.target_specification: Open indicative condition versus explicitly contrary-present preterite subjunctive condition.

items.prompt: Translate each sentence. Distinguish interrogative hwonne, temporal ðonne, and comparative ðonne; do not infer the function from the spelling alone.
items.target_specification: When-question, when-clause and than-standard are distinct functions.

items.prompt: Translate. Who is understood to do the helping in each sentence? Explain why a finite purpose clause can make a different subject explicit.
items.target_specification: Earlier same-subject purposive infinitive contrasted with finite purpose and its own subject.

items.prompt: Translate. Identify the antecedent of ðe and explain why this is neither a direct when-question nor a free-standing conditional.
items.target_specification: Bounded temporal relative after day, needed by Cook V.18.7.

items.prompt: Translate using past ðā … ðā: When the father came, the son gave him water.
items.target_specification: Past temporal correlation with independently governed recipient.

items.prompt: Translate as a recurring event, using ðonne … ðonne: When the fishermen come, the king gives them food.
items.target_specification: Recurring temporal clause and main-clause correlation.

items.prompt: Translate with mid-ðȳ: While the fishermen sat in the house, the son carried water.
items.target_specification: Factual simultaneous past events with a plural temporal subject and a singular main subject.

items.prompt: Address one person. The speaker has not yet arrived. Translate with ǣr: Do not go before I come.
items.target_specification: Negative imperative and anticipated-before subjunctive.

items.prompt: Address several people. The fishermen have not yet arrived. Translate with oð-ðæt: Be in the house until the fishermen come.
items.target_specification: Until with an anticipated plural event, a plural command and an explicit subject.

items.prompt: Translate with for-ðon-ðe and the adjective ðurstig: The monk gives the man water because the man is thirsty.
items.target_specification: Factual cause with indicative and an agreeing predicate adjective.

items.prompt: Translate with a finite ðæt purpose clause: The fishermen came so that the monk might help them.
items.target_specification: Past purpose with a different subordinate subject and a plural dative beneficiary.

items.prompt: Translate the result as an actual past event, using swā … ðæt: The men were so hungry that they ate the food.
items.target_specification: Asserted result with plural indicative and agreeing predicate, distinguished from an intention.

items.prompt: Translate with ðȳ-lǣs-ðe: The fishermen held the animals, lest the animals take our food.
items.target_specification: Negative purpose after a past main clause with plural preterite subjunctive and ordinary lexical objects.

items.prompt: The monk was in fact sick. Translate using the selected concessive pattern: Although the monk was sick, he helped the man.
items.target_specification: Factual concession with the selected preterite subjunctive.

items.prompt: The king is absent now. Translate the contrary-present condition: If the king were here, he would help us.
items.target_specification: Nonpast unreal condition and consequence with preterite subjunctives; no new English-style would auxiliary.

items.prompt: Translate the whole new account The fisherman and his son.
items.target_specification: Connected independent reading with taught vocabulary, reference and clause relations.

items.prompt: In the new account, identify the purpose clause, the while clause and the concession. State what each contributes to the account and parse its finite verb.
items.target_specification: Three adverbial functions in connected narration.

items.prompt: In the new account, who gives the first food, who receives it, and who gives the final water? Explain the relevant pronouns and genitive possessors.
items.target_specification: Track agents, dative recipients and possessors through connected clauses.

items.prompt: In the son’s direct speech, who is ic, when is the coming expected, and what mood is cume? Identify the later action that fulfills the expectation.
items.target_specification: Direct-speech reference, anticipated-until relation and later narrative fulfillment.

items.prompt: Translate: They had built the house. The building is earlier than another past event; use preterite habban with the selected past participle.
items.target_specification: Productive anterior construction with third plural auxiliary.

items.prompt: Translate: The men bound the horse. Then express the horse’s binding as an agentless passive, using preterite weorðan.
items.target_specification: Active accusative object becomes nominative passive subject; change finite number with the new subject.

items.prompt: Translate: The monk says that he is here. Use the subjunctive to present his report. Then put the saying in the past, keeping his presence simultaneous with that past saying.
items.target_specification: Reported sequence with explicit simultaneous relation, retained reference and appropriate finite forms.

items.prompt: Translate: He said that he had built the house. Use the reporting subjunctive and preterite habban with the selected past participle.
items.target_specification: Earlier action within a past report, without mistaking the participle for a finite verb.

items.prompt: Translate: He said that he intended to come. Use willan with the infinitive; do not assert that he actually came.
items.target_specification: Reported intention and its temporal relation, not a mechanical would-to-past rule.

items.prompt: Address one person: Prepare the food. Then translate the reply: I have prepared the food. Use gierwan in both.
items.target_specification: New accusative-object frame and past-participle construction built on the known command and indicative auxiliary.

items.prompt: Translate: The bridge was built. Then a man came. Use an agentless passive with wesan for the completed bridge, followed by a simple preterite for the arrival.
items.target_specification: Passive result followed by narrated event; correct feminine subject and independently inflected arrival verb.

items.prompt: Translate the whole new account, A house and a return. Preserve its changes between narrative, direct speech and reported intention.
items.target_specification: Connected independent interpretation using productive records; no source-only help.

items.prompt: Put these events in order: the son’s first arrival; building the house; the son’s departure; the father’s announcement; the son’s return with food. Which verb phrase places one event before the story’s first arrival?
items.target_specification: Reconstruct connected sequence from finite tense, periphrasis and discourse.

items.prompt: Identify the referents of ic in the father’s speech, hē in the reported intention, and hē in the last sentence. Is the journey an intention only, or does the following narrative show a departure? Cite the relevant words.
items.target_specification: Track reference and distinguish a reported intention from separately narrated fulfillment.

items.prompt: In Nū hæbbe ic ðæt hūs geworht, identify the subject and object. Express the house’s completed state in an agentless sentence with present wesan and the same participle.
items.target_specification: Apply active/passive argument distinction to an understood connected context.

local_support.text: Ælfred is subject. The feminine hīe/hēo refers to bōc. The source-language phrases use of plus dative; on Englisc gives the translation’s goal. Word be worde contrasts literal verbal correspondence with andgiet of andgiete, sense for sense. Gedōn describes the work’s resulting arrangement.

local_support.text: The two superlative adverbs mean “most clearly and most intelligibly.” For plus dative introduces the worldly cares that constrained how clearly Alfred could explain it. local_support.text: The two superlative adverbs mean “most clearly and most intelligibly.” For plus dative introduces the worldly cares that constrained how clearly Alfred could explain it. local_support.text: Ælfred is subject. The feminine hīe/hēo refers to bōc. The source-language phrases use of plus dative; on Englisc gives the translation’s goal. Word be worde contrasts literal verbal correspondence with andgiet of andgiete, sense for sense. Gedōn describes the work’s resulting arrangement.

local_support.text: The two superlative adverbs mean “most clearly and most intelligibly.” For plus dative introduces the worldly cares that constrained how clearly Alfred could explain it. Ǣgðer ge ... ge means “both ... and.” On mōde/on līchaman identify mind and body. Sind is the plural present “are.” The relative ðe at word61 refers to bisga; those cares are the subject of becōmon.

local_support.text: Hæfde underfangen = “had received/taken charge of.” The repeated hæfde governs both geleornod and gewęnd: “had studied ... and translated ...”. Ðēah here is “nevertheless”; ðā ... ðā frames “when ... then.” Tō Engliscum spelle and tō lēoðe mark resulting literary form. Hīe/hēo still refers to the book.

local_support.text: Supply hē (Alfred) with bitt and hālsað, as Cook’s note4 directs. Ǣlcne ðāra ðe ... means “each of those who ...”. Lyste is impersonal: “whom it may please to read this book”; its understood accusative experiencer is the prospective reader. The requested ðæt clause contains subjunctive gebidde, “that he pray for him.”

local_support.text: Ne wīte continues the request: “and not blame him.” In gif hē hit rihtlicor ongiete ðonne hē meahte, the first hē is the reader and the second is Alfred (Cook’s notes6–7). Ongiete is subjunctive; wīte is the verb “blame,” not the noun “punishment.”

local_support.text: Dryhten and God are direct address; ælmihtiga is weak singular. Wyrhta and Wealdend are “Maker and Ruler,” with genitive ealra gesceafta. This Maker sense is distinct from the previously taught workman sense.

local_support.text: The for phrases name grounds of appeal. In ðǣre hālgan rōde tācne, the genitive phrase “of the holy cross” depends on dative tācne. Sanctæ Marian and Sancti Michaeles are supplied names in genitive function with mixed foreign-name inflection; do not derive a new productive Latin paradigm. Gehīersumnesse is obedience. Hālgena means saints; lufan is the weak noun’s dative; earnungum means merits.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: The requested ðæt clause has gewissie, “that you guide.” Bęt ðonne ic āworhte tō ðē means better than my conduct towards you has deserved. The following gewissa is a direct singular command. In mīnre sāwle ðearfe, mīnre sāwle is genitive, dependent on dative ðearfe: “for my soul’s benefit.” Cunne is first-singular subjunctive, “than I myself may know.”
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: Gestaðela, gestranga, āfierr and gescield are addressed singular commands. Establish my mind according to your will; strengthen me against the devil’s temptations; remove lust and unrighteousness; protect me against visible and invisible adversaries. The latter adjectives agree with dative plural wiðerwinnum.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: Tǣc takes dative mē. Its following ðīnne willan is the accusative object of wyrceanne (“to do your will”), as Cook’s note7 specifies. The ðæt clause gives purpose with mæge. Tōforan eallum ðingum means above all things; the two mid phrases give manner: with pure thought and a pure body.

local_support.text: The final causal clause names God as Creator, Redeemer, help, comfort, trust and hope. Sīe is an optative wish, “may there be”; ðē is dative. Ā is repeated three times, followed by tō worulde būtan ǣghwilcum ęnde, “for ever without any end.”

local_support.text: Dryhten and God are direct address; ælmihtiga is weak singular. Wyrhta and Wealdend are “Maker and Ruler,” with genitive ealra gesceafta. This Maker sense is distinct from the previously taught workman sense.

local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: The for phrases name grounds of appeal. In ðǣre hālgan rōde tācne, the genitive phrase “of the holy cross” depends on dative tācne. Sanctæ Marian and Sancti Michaeles are supplied names in genitive function with mixed foreign-name inflection; do not derive a new productive Latin paradigm. Gehīersumnesse is obedience. Hālgena means saints; lufan is the weak noun’s dative; earnungum means merits.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: The requested ðæt clause has gewissie, “that you guide.” Bęt ðonne ic āworhte tō ðē means better than my conduct towards you has deserved. The following gewissa is a direct singular command. In mīnre sāwle ðearfe, mīnre sāwle is genitive, dependent on dative ðearfe: “for my soul’s benefit.” Cunne is first-singular subjunctive, “than I myself may know.”
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: Gestaðela, gestranga, āfierr and gescield are addressed singular commands. Establish my mind according to your will; strengthen me against the devil’s temptations; remove lust and unrighteousness; protect me against visible and invisible adversaries. The latter adjectives agree with dative plural wiðerwinnum.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: Tǣc takes dative mē. Its following ðīnne willan is the accusative object of wyrceanne (“to do your will”), as Cook’s note7 specifies. The ðæt clause gives purpose with mæge. Tōforan eallum ðingum means above all things; the two mid phrases give manner: with pure thought and a pure body.
local_support.origin_category: new teaching material explaining exact source
local_support.display_obligation: Keep this exact help visible beside every assigned task and during its assessment; no independent recall of supplied material is tested.

local_support.text: The final causal clause names God as Creator, Redeemer, help, comfort, trust and hope. Sīe is an optative wish, “may there be”; ðē is dative. Ā is repeated three times, followed by tō worulde būtan ǣghwilcum ęnde, “for ever without any end.”

Translate both clauses, using plegian for the first two expressed actions and dōn for the final repeated action: The men played well; the king played better than they did. Explain what the last verb replaces and why it is plural.

items.prompt: Analyse the report. The man’s goodness is presented as simultaneous with the king’s past statement.

outputs.label: Identify the two subjects and their finite verbs.

outputs.label: Classify ðæt and explain the reported time relation.

outputs.label: Does wǣre require the conclusion that the man was not good? Explain.
outputs.essential_meaning: Separate reporting mood from truth value.

outputs.label: Translate the sentence.
outputs.essential_meaning: Preserve the direction of comparison and both singers.

outputs.label: State the action repeated by dyde and explain why it is singular.
outputs.essential_meaning: The comparison clause has independent agreement.

outputs.label: Write the complete revised Old English sentence.
outputs.essential_meaning: Change the first subject/article and sang to plural, preserving the second clause.

outputs.essential_meaning: Distinguish internal relative subject from antecedent accusative.

outputs.label: Write the complete revised Old English sentence.
outputs.essential_meaning: Plural antecedent and plural relative verb; first-person seeing remains singular.

items.prompt: A concerns a possible visit tomorrow. In B the speaker treats his coming now as contrary to fact. Analyse both clauses in each sentence.

outputs.label: Translate A and name the mood of each verb.
outputs.essential_meaning: Open future condition with contextually future present indicatives.

outputs.label: Translate B and name the tense and mood of each verb.
outputs.essential_meaning: Morphological preterite subjunctive with a specified contrary-present use.

outputs.label: Explain which evidence supplies the time and factual status.
outputs.essential_meaning: Context controls interpretation beyond a conjunction label.

items.prompt: Use cniht in its explicitly taught servant sense and bōc book. Translate the four expressions. In each, choose the noun's case from its role rather than from an English word ending.

outputs.label: the servant's book
outputs.essential_meaning: One servant possesses one book.

outputs.label: the servants' books
outputs.essential_meaning: Several servants possess several books.

outputs.label: I give the servant the book.
outputs.essential_meaning: The speaker gives one book to one servant.

outputs.label: We give the servants the books.
outputs.essential_meaning: The speakers give several books to several servants.

items.prompt: Use the selected endingless accusative of cwēn queen, while retaining its genitive/dative ending. Translate the three expressions, then explain the contrast.

outputs.label: I saw the queen.
outputs.essential_meaning: The queen is the person seen.

outputs.label: I gave the queen the book.
outputs.essential_meaning: The queen receives the book.

outputs.label: the queen's book
outputs.essential_meaning: A book belonging to the queen.

outputs.label: Explain what the three queen forms show about identifying case from an ending alone.
outputs.essential_meaning: Case is governed by the whole construction; the selected accusative is endingless, and genitive/dative share an ending.

items.prompt: Use fox fox, hol hole and nest nest. Translate each sentence. Keep ordinary locative on with the dative and distinguish the two neuter plural patterns.

outputs.label: The fox is in the hole.
outputs.essential_meaning: One fox is located in one hole.

outputs.label: The foxes are in the holes.
outputs.essential_meaning: Several foxes are located in several holes.

outputs.label: The nest is in the tree.
outputs.essential_meaning: One nest is located in one tree.

outputs.label: The nests are in the trees.
outputs.essential_meaning: Several nests are located in several trees.

outputs.label: The holes are large.
outputs.essential_meaning: Several holes are large.

items.prompt: Use hęrian praise. Supply only the finite form required in each stated setting, then explain the contrast. The dictionary form is visible reference help.

outputs.label: A narrator states: they praise. Give present indicative third plural.
outputs.essential_meaning: An assertion of several people's praising.

outputs.label: A speaker commands several listeners: praise! Give second-plural imperative.
outputs.essential_meaning: A direct command to several addressees.

outputs.label: A speaker wishes: may they praise. Give present subjunctive third plural.
outputs.essential_meaning: A third-person wish.

outputs.label: Which answers are spelled alike, and what distinguishes their functions?
outputs.essential_meaning: The present indicative plural and plural imperative share a surface; asserted subject versus commanded addressee and context distinguish them.

items.prompt: Use the explicitly taught present participles of ondrǣdan fear and hyngran be hungry. Translate the two nominal phrases, then distinguish each phrase's outer case from any object governed inside it.

outputs.label: to those fearing him: use a dative plural participle without an expressed people noun; him is the one feared
outputs.essential_meaning: The beneficiaries are the people who fear him.

outputs.label: the hungry: give the weak accusative plural phrase used as a direct object
outputs.essential_meaning: The hungry people are the direct object.

outputs.label: State the two grammatical relations in the fear phrase.
outputs.essential_meaning: The participle phrase is dative as beneficiary, while ondrǣdan governs the accusative object within it.

outputs.label: Explain why a present participle can name people here without being a finite verb.
outputs.essential_meaning: The participial form is used nominally for people characterized by the activity or condition; its case follows the noun phrase's role, and no independent finite verb is present.

items.prompt: After translating Cook 43.1, analyse both images. Keep your complete translation beside the English prompt and the supplied vocabulary.

outputs.label: Identify the two things joined by the first copular image and explain its contextual force.
outputs.essential_meaning: Distinguish literal copular structure from the contextual comparison.

outputs.label: Identify the second comparison and distinguish its structure from the first.
outputs.essential_meaning: Preserve both the flesh/grass image and the glory/blossom comparison.

outputs.label: Explain why Human life is brief alone is not a complete translation of 43.1.
outputs.essential_meaning: Separate translation from interpretive paraphrase.

outputs.essential_meaning: Contextual horn sense without loss of literal image.

outputs.label: For 40.9, explain what seed denotes and identify whose seed it is.
outputs.essential_meaning: Explicit new collective descendants sense and correct possessor.

outputs.label: State what the familiar inflection alone cannot establish in these two examples.
outputs.essential_meaning: Form knowledge and sense knowledge are separate.

items.prompt: Translate the complete assigned reading in the three stated divisions, keeping all local help available.

outputs.label: Translate 174.7–174.13, through tǣlst.
outputs.essential_meaning: She has her harp fetched, sings and plays; everyone praises her except silent Apollonius; the king treats his silence as censure.

outputs.label: Translate 174.14–175.2, through wel gelǣred.
outputs.essential_meaning: Apollonius asks permission, says the daughter has chanced upon music but not learned it well, requests the harp and promises a demonstration; the king acknowledges his learning.

outputs.label: Translate 175.3–175.17, through the final forðtēah.
outputs.essential_meaning: The king orders the harp given; Apollonius changes dress and performs; listeners mistake his appearance for Apollo, then praise his music and unfamiliar performances.

items.prompt: Identify each referent and the grammatical evidence. Use the supplied source notes; say when context is needed.

outputs.label: Give the referent of hēo in 174.7.
outputs.essential_meaning: The king’s daughter, supplied by preceding English context.

outputs.label: Give the referent of hine in 174.16 and its role.
outputs.essential_meaning: The musical art, masculine swēgcræft; accusative object of learned, not the king or Apollonius.

outputs.label: Give the referent of hē in the reported clauses 175.7–8.
outputs.essential_meaning: Apollonius as perceived by the audience; their identification is embedded in thought.

outputs.label: Give the referent and case of him eallum in 175.16–17.
outputs.essential_meaning: All the listeners; dative experiencers with līcode, not the grammatical subject.

items.prompt: Identify the clause relationship in each cited expression and distinguish it from a similar construction elsewhere.

outputs.label: Classify sōna swā 174.8 and explain its time relation.
outputs.essential_meaning: As soon as: the beginning of playing is followed immediately by the accompanying song.

outputs.label: Classify gif 174.14–15 in its context.
outputs.essential_meaning: A permission condition introducing a courteous request to speak; no contrary-to-fact meaning is required.

outputs.label: Classify swā … ðæt 175.6–7.
outputs.essential_meaning: Manner/degree followed by result: his appearance makes the audience take him for Apollo.

outputs.label: Explain why the two ðæt clauses 175.7–8 do not assert that Apollonius actually is Apollo.
outputs.essential_meaning: They are the contents of what the king and bystanders thought; the two clauses contrast their identifications.

items.prompt: Analyse the supplied participial and predicate expressions without changing the source spelling.

outputs.label: Explain swīgende 174.13 using original note 12a.
outputs.essential_meaning: The edition’s form stands for swīgiende, a present participle accompanying the addressee’s silence/censure; preserve the actual printed spelling.

outputs.label: Explain the referent of ðā ymbsittendan 175.7.
outputs.essential_meaning: The people sitting around: a substantival participial expression for the bystanders.

outputs.label: Account for singular ungecnāwen wæs and ungewunelic 175.16.
outputs.essential_meaning: Preserve the source’s collective/singular construal of the presented performances after fela…ðinga; do not silently regularize the text to plural.

outputs.label: Identify the subject of līcode 175.17 and distinguish it from him eallum.
outputs.essential_meaning: Ǣlc of the performances is the singular subject; him eallum is the dative experiencer.

items.prompt: Separate literal wording from the contextual performance sense in each expression, using the local help and original notes.

outputs.label: Explain gefēoll on swēgcræft 174.16.
outputs.essential_meaning: Literally fell upon musical art; in context chanced upon/took up music, contrasted with not having learned it well.

outputs.label: Explain plegode and forðtēah 175.15.
outputs.essential_meaning: Performed/acted and presented performances; the note’s Latin explains comic/tragic acting, while the Old English wording remains broader.

outputs.label: Explain the function of Apollines 175.8.
outputs.essential_meaning: The name identifies Apollo in the listeners’ mistaken comparison; preserve the narrator’s report rather than translating an actual transformation.

items.prompt: Explain the argument of the episode from the actual Old English.

outputs.label: State the difference between the king’s reading of silence and Apollonius’s explanation.
outputs.essential_meaning: The king treats silence as blame; Apollonius explains that the daughter has not mastered her musical art.

outputs.label: Identify two kinds of evidence by which Apollonius answers the criticism of his conduct.
outputs.essential_meaning: He demonstrates skilled music, then further striking performances; the audience’s praise and pleasure validate his demonstrated ability.

outputs.label: Explain how the final sentence combines novelty with approval.
outputs.essential_meaning: The performances were unfamiliar and unusual to the audience, yet each pleased all the listeners; unfamiliarity does not express disapproval here.
